hook: The codebreaker who helped win the Second World War and imagined the modern computer.

pages.x: Alan Turing was born in London in 1912. At 13, on his first day at a new school, there was a general strike and no trains, so he cycled about 100 km on his own to get there.

In 1936, at 24, he imagined a simple machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape, following a list of rules. He showed that such a machine could carry out any calculation that can be done step by step.
pages.fx: It is the idea behind every computer: one machine that can do any task, given the right program.

pages.x: In the Second World War, at Bletchley Park, he led the team that broke the codes of the German navy's Enigma machines, and designed the Bombe, a machine that found each day's settings.
Reading the messages of the German submarines helped the Allies win the Battle of the Atlantic. Historians think the codebreakers shortened the war by perhaps two years, saving millions of lives.
He chained his tea mug to a radiator so no one would take it, wore a gas mask in June to keep off hay fever, and ran marathons, almost fast enough for the 1948 Olympics.

After the war he designed one of the first computers that stored its own programs, and in 1950 asked "Can machines think?" He proposed a test: can a machine chat so well that you cannot tell it from a person?
pages.fx: It started the field of artificial intelligence, and the Turing test is still argued about today.

pages.x: In 1952 he was convicted because he was gay, then a crime in Britain, and forced to take hormone injections. In 1954 he died of cyanide poisoning, ruled a suicide. He was 41.
In 2009 the British prime minister apologised for how he had been treated. In 2013 he was pardoned, and since 2021 his face has been on the 50-pound note.
Turing is a father of computer science and of artificial intelligence, and his codebreaking helped win the Second World War.
pts: Invented the idea of the universal computer
Started the field of artificial intelligence
